Hi! I'm Dr. Kelvin. Tap any movement below to control me on the whiteboard!
Spin and steer a balanced plastic straw through empty air without ever touching it with your hands.
A plastic straw balanced on the neck of a glass bottle rotates and follows your charged wand across the air as if controlled by telekinesis.

Rubbing a plastic wand transfers electrons via the triboelectric effect, accumulating negative charge (-Q). When brought close to the uncharged straw, it induces electric polarization: electrons in the straw are repelled to the far side, leaving a net positive charge on the near side. The resulting electrostatic attraction creates a net torque (tau = r x F) about the balance point.

Balance a lightweight plastic straw across the top of a glass bottle or upside-down cup. Rub another straw, plastic ruler, or balloon vigorously against a wool sweater or dry hair, then bring it near the end of the balanced straw.
Squeeze an orange peel near an inflated balloon and watch it pop instantaneously without touching.
Simply squeezing a fresh orange or lemon peel a few inches away from a balloon instantly pops it with a loud bang, without needles or flames.

The skin of citrus fruits contains tiny reservoirs of d-limonene, an organic hydrocarbon oil. Latex rubber balloons are composed of cross-linked polyisoprene chains held under extreme mechanical tensile stress. Under the chemistry rule of \'like dissolves like\', the non-polar limonene instantly dissolves the non-polar latex polymer bonds upon contact, causing rapid catastrophic crack propagation at the speed of sound in rubber (~50 m/s)!

Blow up a latex balloon until it is tightly inflated. Cut a piece of orange or lemon peel. Hold the peel with the colored rind facing the balloon, squeeze it sharply to express the citrus oil mist, and watch it pop!
Poke sharp pencils straight through a water-filled plastic bag without spilling a single drop!
Poking sharp pencils through a water bag seems like it should instantly cause water to burst out everywhere, yet not a single drop leaks!

Plastic zipper sandwich bags are made of High-Density Polyethylene (HDPE) or Low-Density Polyethylene (LDPE). These are long chains of repeating polymer molecules. When pierced by a smooth, sharp pencil tip, the flexible polymer chains separate and stretch tightly around the shaft of the pencil like rubber bands, forming a watertight temporary gasket.
Hydrostatic Pressure vs. Polymer Hoop Stress
Fill a clean zip-lock bag 3/4 full with water and seal it. Sharpen 4-6 round pencils. With one smooth, steady motion, poke each pencil through one side and out the other over a sink or bowl!
Submerge a glass tube into a liquid and watch its contours vanish completely before your eyes.
When immersed in a clear mystery fluid, a real solid glass tube completely vanishes from sight, as if it dissolved into nothingness.

We see transparent glass because light reflects and refracts at the boundary between the surrounding medium and the glass due to differing speeds of light (refractive index n). Pyrex borosilicate glass has n â 1.474. When submerged in vegetable oil or glycerin (which also has n â 1.47), the light travels at the exact same speed in both. Light neither bends nor reflects at the boundary, making the glass 100% invisible!

Take a Pyrex glass stirring rod or small Pyrex test tube and place it in a cup of plain water (it will be visible). Now place it in a cup of clear vegetable cooking oil or glycerinâit disappears entirely!
Command a submarine diver inside a sealed water bottle to dive, hover, and surface using your hands.
By merely squeezing the outside of a sealed plastic bottle, an object floating quietly at the top suddenly dives to the bottom on command, and floats back up when you let go.

Named after RenÃ© Descartes. The diver contains a trapped bubble of air. Squeezing the bottle transmits pressure equally throughout the fluid (Pascal\'s law). The increased pressure compresses the trapped air bubble (Boyle\'s law: PÂ·V = const), reducing its displaced volume. When average density exceeds water, gravity overcomes buoyant force and it sinks.
Attach modeling clay to a plastic pen cap until it barely floats upright in a cup of water. Place inside a 2L bottle filled to the brim with water, cap tightly, and squeeze!
A liquid you can run across, but will swallow your foot if you stand still for a second.
When struck hard with a hammer or punched quickly, this strange white liquid behaves like rock-solid armor; but relax your hand, and it flows like water through your fingers.

A suspension of cornstarch in water is a dilatant (shear-thickening) non-Newtonian fluid. Under low shear rates, water lubricates the starch granules. Under sudden high shear stress, the lubricating water is squeezed out from between particles, causing friction and mechanical jamming into a temporary solid lattice.
Mix 2 cups of cornstarch with 1 cup of tap water in a bowl. Tap the surface rapidly with your spoon, then slowly rest your spoon into it!
Hover a lightweight ball inside an invisible stream of angled air without dropping.
A ping pong ball levitates stably in mid-air above a hairdryerâeven when the nozzle is tilted at a steep 45-degree angle!

Bernoulli\'s principle states that faster-moving air creates lower static pressure. As high-speed air rushes past the ball, the static pressure inside the stream drops below ambient room pressure. If the ball tries to leave the airstream, higher external atmospheric pressure pushes it back in.
Turn on a hairdryer on cool air. Place a ping pong ball into the upward stream and slowly tilt the dryer up to 45 degrees!
Aim a cannon and launch projectiles against quadratic aerodynamic drag and crosswinds.
In introductory physics, balls fly in symmetrical parabolas. In reality, aerodynamic drag makes balls drop steeply near the end and fall short.

Real air creates aerodynamic skin friction and form drag proportional to velocity squared: F_drag = 0.5 * rho * C_d * A * |v_rel|^2, directed opposite to relative motion. Combined with gravity and wind gusts, equations of motion become coupled nonlinear differential equations.
Newton\'s 2nd Law with Quadratic Drag & Wind
Drop a flat sheet of paper and a crumpled paper ball simultaneously. The crumpled ball hits first due to lower cross-sectional area and drag!
Drop a ball from customizable heights and observe height decay, floor deformation, and live kinetic vs potential energy graphs.
A rubber ball bounced on a hard floor never returns to its initial drop height, continuously losing bounce height until coming to a silent rest.

During impact, the ball deforms elastically and converts mechanical kinetic energy into internal thermal energy and sound vibrations. The ratio of rebound speed to impact speed is the coefficient of restitution e = v_rebound / v_impact <= 1.0.
Newton\'s Coefficient of Restitution & Energy Decay
Drop a cold tennis ball versus a warm tennis ball onto a hard kitchen tile and compare the bounce heights!
Pull back 1, 2, or 3 steel balls and watch compression shockwaves propagate instantly through the chain.
If you release 2 balls into 5 stationary balls, exactly 2 balls pop out the other side at the exact same speed, never 1 ball with double speed!
Simultaneous conservation of linear momentum (sum m*v) and kinetic energy (sum 0.5*m*v^2) strictly uniquely constrains the number of departing spheres and their velocities during elastic impacts.
Line up 5 identical coins touching on a smooth table. Flick a coin hard into one end; watch only the single coin at the far end shoot away!
Race balls down a straight ramp, circular arc, and cycloid curve to prove the straight line is NOT the fastest!
A ball rolling down a curved cycloid ramp beats a ball rolling down a straight ramp between the exact same start and end points every single time.

Solved by Johann Bernoulli in 1696 using the calculus of variations and Snell\'s Law analogy. The cycloid curve accelerates the ball rapidly at the start, building up early kinetic energy and speed that reduces total travel time.
Build two tracks out of flexible plastic pipe: one straight slant and one dipping down steeply first. Roll marbles down both simultaneously!
Drop skydivers from 4,000 meters, toggle body orientations, and deploy parachutes to observe velocity equilibrium.
No matter how high you jump from an airplane, you stop accelerating after about 12 seconds and fall at a steady constant speed.
As speed increases, upward aerodynamic drag grows until it precisely balances downward gravity force (F_net = 0). At this point acceleration is zero and the object falls at terminal velocity v_t.
Drop a single paper cupcake liner versus a stack of 4 liners nested together. The stack falls faster because mass is 4x while area A remains the same!
Pull a heavy sled with an elastic spring and observe sudden jerky slip-stick oscillations.
Pulling a heavy box with a rubber band causes it to jerk and shudder in rhythmic leaps rather than sliding smoothly across the floor.

Static friction coefficient mu_s is strictly greater than kinetic friction coefficient mu_k. As pulling force builds up, the object sticks until F > mu_s * N. Once sliding begins, resistance drops to mu_k * N, causing a sudden acceleration and overshoot.
Push a heavy book across a table using just the tip of your index finger slowly. Notice the micro-shudders and jerks as it moves!
Rig 1, 2, 4, or 8 pulley wheels to lift extreme 1,000 kg loads using the strength of a single hand.
Adding simple spinning wheels with a rope allows a child to lift an engine block with barely any effort.

In an ideal pulley system, cable tension T is uniform throughout. When an object is supported by n vertical rope segments, the upward force is n * T, multiplying input force by ideal mechanical advantage n at the cost of pulling n times more rope.
Thread a rope around two broomsticks held by two friends. You alone can pull the two sticks together even if both friends resist with all their strength!
Steer a planet around a gravitational star. Adjust eccentricity, observe velocity vector changes, and visualize Kepler\'s equal areas law!
Planets do not orbit in simple circles, nor do they travel at constant speeds. They speed up whip-fast near the sun and cruise slowly far away.

Under Newton\'s law of universal gravitation, an inverse-square central force conserves orbital angular momentum L = r x (m v). Kepler\'s Second Law proves the radius vector sweeps out equal sector areas in equal intervals of time (dA/dt = L / 2m = constant).
Tie a small weight to a string and swing it in an ellipse. Watch how your hand must apply more tension when passing closest to the center!
Spin a heavy bicycle wheel supported by a single string and observe how it rotates sideways instead of falling down.
A spinning wheel suspended from only one side refuses to topple over under gravity, instead precessing horizontally in a circle.

When a body with large angular momentum L is subjected to a gravitational torque tau = r x F_g, the torque vector is perpendicular to L. According to tau = dL/dt, the torque changes the direction of L rather than its magnitude, causing steady horizontal precession.
Spin a child\'s toy gyroscope on the tip of a pencil. Notice how it leans without falling over!
Fictitious Forces on Rotating Reference Frames
Throw a ball across a rotating carousel and watch its path curve dramatically from the spinning observer\'s view.
Throwing a ball straight to a friend across a spinning playground merry-go-round causes the ball to swerve sideways in mid-air!

In a rotating reference frame rotating at angular velocity Omega, moving objects experience an apparent fictitious acceleration a_coriolis = -2 * (Omega x v) due to the frame\'s changing tangential velocity with radius.
Place a marble on a rotating Lazy Susan turntable and roll it outward. Notice how its path traces an outward spiral curve!
Fly a spacecraft behind a moving giant planet and catapult into interstellar space with massive kinetic velocity gain.
A spacecraft can speed up by thousands of kilometers per hour without firing an engine, simply by flying near Jupiter!

In the planet\'s reference frame, the encounter is an elastic hyperbolic scatter with zero energy change. In the Sun\'s frame, the probe gains up to twice the planet\'s orbital velocity: v_final = v_in + 2 * v_planet.
Drop a tennis ball with a small bouncy superball resting directly on top. Upon hitting the floor, the top ball shoots upward to extreme heights!
Day 19: Roche Limit & Tidal Ring Creation
Send a moon orbiting too close to a gas giant and watch planetary tidal forces rip it into glowing rings like Saturn.
If a moon drifts too close to its host planet, the planet\'s gravity doesn\'t pull it into a crashâit tears the moon apart into billions of pieces.

The differential tidal gravitational force between the moon\'s near side and far side exceeds the moon\'s internal self-gravitational cohesion at the Roche limit d = 2.44 * R * (rho_M / rho_m)^(1/3), disrupting it into a ring disk.
Look up photos of Saturn\'s ringsâthey are the pulverized debris of ancient icy moons that crossed Saturn\'s Roche limit!
Park telescopes at Earth-Sun L1 and L2 points and observe how gravitational pull and centrifugal force balance perfectly.
There are five special invisible islands in empty space where spacecraft can park forever with virtually zero fuel.

In a circular restricted two-body system, the effective gravitational-centrifugal potential forms five stationary points where net force in the rotating frame is zero. L4 and L5 form stable triangular equilateral points.
Research how the James Webb Space Telescope orbits the invisible Earth-Sun L2 Lagrange point 1.5 million km away!
Simulate 3 gravitational stars: discover periodic figure-8 orbits, Lagrange points, and violent chaotic stellar ejections.
While two orbiting bodies have exact mathematical solutions, adding just one more body renders the system mathematically unsolvable by closed-form equations.

The general three-body problem exhibits non-integrability discovered by Henri PoincarÃ©. Small orbital perturbations can sling one star out into deep interstellar space while the remaining two form an eccentric binary pair.
Look up the famous Figure-8 three-body orbit discovered in 1993, where three equal stars chase each other along a single figure-eight loop!
Touch and pluck a taut musical string anywhere along its length. Watch wave packets reflect, invert at boundaries, and form standing harmonic nodes!
Plucking a guitar string at one tiny point creates complex harmonic waves traveling back and forth, producing pure musical tones and standing node patterns.

A string with tension T and linear mass density mu satisfies the classical 1D wave equation u_tt = c^2 u_xx, where c = sqrt(T / mu) is the propagation speed. Fixed boundaries enforce u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0, causing wave pulses to invert upon reflection.
Stretch a long rubber band between your fingers. Flick it sharply to see the wave pulse travel to the fixed end, invert upside down, and bounce back!
Synthesize square, sawtooth, and triangle waveforms using rotating epicyclic circles. Watch individual Fourier harmonics sum together in real time!
How can a bunch of smooth, round rotating circles and pure sine tones combine to create sharp square corners, jagged sawtooths, and complex sound timbres?

Fourier\'s theorem proves that any periodic function can be represented as an infinite sum of sinusoidal harmonics with integer multiple frequencies n*omega. Truncating to finite harmonics produces the famous ~9% overshoot known as Gibbs Phenomenon.
Download an audio spectrum analyzer app on your phone. Play a pure sine wave, then a square wave, and watch the ladder of odd harmonic spikes!
Vibrate a square plate at resonant frequencies and watch thousands of grains of sand organize into intricate geometric patterns.
Sand scattered randomly across a metal sheet instantly dances into breathtaking mandalas and sacred geometric figures when a violin bow strikes the edge.

Standing flexural waves in a thin elastic 2D plate produce stationary nodal lines where plate displacement is identically zero. Sand bouncing off vibrating regions naturally gathers into these zero-amplitude nodal lines.
Sprinkle fine salt on plastic wrap stretched tightly over a speaker cone. Play tones from 200 Hz to 1000 Hz and watch geometric lines appear!
Tune an acoustic tone to the exact resonant frequency of a crystal wine glass until mechanical stress shatters the rim.
A singer producing a single pure note at matching pitch causes a crystal glass across the room to shake violently and shatter into pieces without physical contact.

At resonance, the driving audio frequency matches the glass\'s natural eigenmode. Because glass has a high quality factor (Q), energy builds up with each cycle until hoop stresses exceed the tensile strength of silica.
Wet your index finger and rub it around the rim of a crystal wine glass to make it sing with a ringing resonant tone!
Accelerate a wave source past Mach 1.0 and witness how compressed circular wavefronts fuse into a conical sonic boom shockwave.
As an airplane exceeds the speed of sound, all sound waves emitted pile up into a razor-thin shockwave cone, creating a thunderous ground blast.
Moving wave sources compress wavelengths ahead and stretch them behind. At supersonic speed (v > c), wavefront spheres overlap constructively along a cone with half-angle sin(theta) = 1 / Mach.
Listen to an ambulance or train horn speed past you: notice how the pitch drops instantly the moment it passes your ears!
Play two frequencies just 2 Hz apart and hear a periodic wobbling volume beat caused by wave superposition.
Playing two pure tones of 440 Hz and 442 Hz produces a distinct rhythmic thrumming sound at 2 beats per second.

When two waves with frequencies f1 and f2 superpose, trigonometric identity cos(a) + cos(b) = 2 cos((a-b)/2) cos((a+b)/2) reveals a carrier frequency with a slowly oscillating amplitude envelope of beat frequency f_beat = |f1 - f2|.
Hum a steady note while playing a guitar string that is slightly out of tune with your voice: hear the rhythmic pulsating beats!
Expose a suspension bridge to 40 mph crosswinds and watch aeroelastic flutter amplify twisting vibrations until total structural failure.
A giant steel and concrete bridge twisted like a ribbon in a moderate breeze and tore itself apart in 1940.

Wind flow separated around the H-shaped deck creating alternating vortex shedding. When torsional deck twisting altered aerodynamic angles, aerodynamic forces fed mechanical energy into the oscillation, creating catastrophic aeroelastic flutter.
Hold a strip of paper loosely between two fingers and blow air over the top: notice how it vibrates frantically in self-excited flutter!
Bending laser beams inside an arcing water stream without escaping.
Light travels in straight linesâyet shining a laser into an arcing water stream bends light along the falling water jet!
When light inside water strikes the air boundary at an angle greater than critical angle theta_c = 48.8 deg, 100% of light undergoes total internal reflection.
Poke a hole near the bottom of a water bottle, shine a laser through the other side into the draining stream in a dark room!
Adjust nanometer soap film thickness and watch shimmering iridescent rainbow hues appear.
A completely clear soap bubble develops swirling vibrant rainbow colors without a drop of pigment or dye.
Light reflecting from outer and inner bubble surfaces interferes constructively or destructively depending on film thickness and wavelength.
Dip a wire loop in soapy water and observe rainbow stripes as gravity thins the top!
Pass coherent laser light through twin sub-millimeter slits to produce alternating bright and dark fringe bands.
Shooting a single light beam through two slits produces a ladder of many bright spots on the wall instead of just two lines.
Diffracted circular wavelets from both slits superpose constructively at paths differing by integer wavelengths (d sin theta = m lambda) and destructively at half-wavelengths.
Shine a red laser pointer through the fine gap between two razor blade edges taped tightly together in a dark room!
Split pure white light into a rainbow spectrum through an equilateral glass prism.
A clear triangular block of glass transforms plain white sunlight into seven brilliant rainbow colors.
Glass has a higher refractive index for short-wavelength violet light (n = 1.53) than long-wavelength red light (n = 1.51), bending violet light more sharply.
Shine a flashlight through a clear glass tumbler of water onto a sheet of white paper in sunlight!
Cross two 90Â° polarizing sheets to block 100% light; insert a 45Â° filter between them and watch light reappear!
Blocking all light with two crossed filters can be reversed by putting a third filter in betweenâadding an obstacle lets light through!

Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave. The first filter passes vertical E-field. The 45Â° middle filter projects a diagonal component, which now has a non-zero horizontal projection through the third filter!
Hold two polarized sunglass lenses crossed at 90Â° (blackout), then slide a third polarized lens angled between them!
Multi-Slit Angular Dispersion & Atomic Emission Lines
Resolve elemental spectral emission lines using a precision diffraction grating of 1,000 lines/mm.
Looking at a fluorescent bulb through a CD disc separates light into discrete glowing colored needle lines rather than a continuous rainbow.
Constructive interference across thousands of parallel periodic grating grooves produces razor-sharp angular peaks for each distinct atomic wavelength.
Reflect a flashlight off the grooved recording surface of a DVD or CD disc to see crisp spectral emission lines!
Continuous Refractive Index Gradients in Hot Air
Simulate highway desert mirages where shimmering pools of water appear on scorching asphalt.
A hot desert road looks like it is covered in reflective pools of water, but it is completely bone dry.
Intensely heated air directly above road asphalt has lower density and lower refractive index. Light rays from the sky bend upward into the driver\'s eyes, mimicking a reflection from water.
Look along the surface of an iron baking sheet placed in a hot oven: observe the distorted shimmering horizon line!
Spin a soccer ball and observe how spinning boundary layers deflect airflow and curve the trajectory.
A soccer player kicks a ball straight, and mid-flight it hooks sharply around a defensive wall into the top corner.
A rotating cylinder in airflow drags air faster on one side (lower pressure) and retards air on the other side (higher pressure), generating a perpendicular Magnus lift force.
Drop a light cardboard cup wrapped with a rubber band while giving it rapid backspin: watch it swoop forward and upward!
Launch self-stabilizing toroidal smoke rings that travel meters across a room without dispersing.
A puff of smoke pushed through a round hole forms a spinning donut ring that flies straight like a solid bullet.
Frictional drag at the orifice perimeter rolls the emerging jet into a torus with circulating velocity field. By Kelvin\'s circulation theorem, inviscid vortex lines remain locked with the fluid.
Cut a circular hole in the bottom of a paper cup. Cover the top with plastic wrap, tap the plastic, and blow out a candle 1 meter away!
Drop liquid dish soap onto the stern of a miniature paper boat and watch it blast across water.
Touching a toothpick dipped in dish soap to the water behind a paper cutout shoots it forward like a motorboat.
Water has high surface tension (72 mN/m), while soap lowers it (25 mN/m). The resulting surface tension gradient creates a strong shear stress pulling fluid and boat forward.
Cut a small boat shape out of index card with a notch in the rear. Place in water, dab dish soap in the notch!
Constrict fluid pipe diameter and watch static pressure drop dramatically in the narrow throat.
Forcing water through a constricted narrow pipe causes its internal pressure to plummet rather than climb.
By mass continuity A1*v1 = A2*v2, fluid must accelerate in the narrow throat. By Bernoulli\'s equation, increased kinetic energy density requires an equal drop in static pressure.
Blow air horizontally across the top of an open vertical drinking straw submerged in a cup of water to create an atomizer spray!
Apply a small input force on a narrow piston and crush heavy steel blocks with fluid power.
A child pushing down a small syringe lever can easily lift a 50 kg weight on a connected large syringe.
Pascal\'s principle states pressure applied to an enclosed fluid transmits equally in all directions. Equal pressure P1 = P2 implies F2 = F1 * (A2 / A1).
Connect a small plastic syringe to a large syringe with a tube filled with water. Feel how easily the small one lifts weights on the large!
Dip glass capillary tubes of varying diameters into water and watch fluid defy gravity to climb upward.
Water spontaneously climbs up narrow glass tubes against the downward pull of gravity.
Adhesive forces between polar water molecules and glass silica exceed cohesive forces among water molecules. The curved meniscus creates a Laplace pressure deficit pulling water up.
Dip the corner of a paper towel into colored water: watch the fluid climb vertically up the fibers against gravity!
Laminar to Turbulent Wake Shedding & Strouhal Number
Place a cylinder in flowing water and watch alternating swirling vortices shed into a symmetrical street.
Water flowing past a bridge pier forms an alternating mesmerizing zig-zag train of swirling whirlpools.
At Reynolds numbers between 47 and 10^5, boundary layer separation from top and bottom surfaces alternates periodically, shedding counter-rotating vortices governed by Strouhal number St.
Drag a pencil slowly through a sink filled with calm water illuminated by an overhead light to see the vortex street wake!
Day 43: Ideal Gas Piston & p-V Work
Compress gas particles with a draggable piston and track real-time p-V work and temperature change.
Compressing air rapidly inside a closed cylinder causes its temperature to spike scorchingly hot without external fire.
Doing mechanical work W = integral p dV compresses particles, increasing mean molecular kinetic energy and temperature under adiabatic conditions.
1st Law of Thermodynamics & Ideal Gas Law
Rapidly pump a bicycle hand pump with your thumb sealing the nozzle: feel the metal cylinder barrel get scorching hot!
Track the microscopic random walk of pollen grains bombarded by invisible thermal water molecules.
Microscopic pollen grains in calm water dance and jiggle erratically forever without stopping.
Einstein proved in 1905 that statistical fluctuations in thermal kinetic collisions of water molecules impart random momentum impulses, confirming atomic reality.
Shine a laser pointer through milk diluted with water in a dark room: watch the shimmering erratic jitter of suspended fat droplets!
Heat a pan past 200Â°C and watch water droplets glide effortlessly on an insulating steam cushion.
On a 120Â°C pan water boils away instantly; but on a 220Â°C pan it hovers and glides like an air hockey puck for over a minute!
Instantaneous vaporization beneath the drop forms a micro-layer of steam with very low thermal conductivity, insulating the remaining droplet and providing frictionless gliding.
Heat a clean skillet until hot. Flick water droplets onto it and watch them bead up and skate frictionlessly!
Drive an interactive flywheel using hot expansion and cold compression pistons in a closed gas cycle.
An engine powered solely by resting on top of a hot cup of coffee spins a mechanical flywheel smoothly for hours.
A fixed mass of gas shuttles between hot and cold reservoirs via a regenerator. Constant volume heating and isothermal expansion convert thermal heat differences into mechanical shaft work.
Look up tabletop low-temperature-difference Stirling engines that run entirely on the heat of your palm!
Simulate a microscopic gatekeeper sorting fast particles left and slow particles right to create a temperature difference.
Could an intelligent microscopic creature sort hot and cold atoms without doing work, violating the 2nd Law of Thermodynamics?
Szilard and Landauer showed the demon must measure, record, and eventually erase particle information. Erasing 1 bit of thermodynamic entropy dissipates at least k_B T ln(2) of heat energy.
Explore how modern computer memory chips dissipate heat fundamentally due to Landauer\'s thermodynamic erasure limit!
Day 48: Fourier Heat Conduction in Solids
Apply a blowtorch to one side of a composite metal bar and watch heat diffuse through copper, steel, and wood.
Touching a wooden spoon in boiling soup is painless, but a silver spoon burns your fingers in 5 seconds.
Heat flux q is proportional to the negative thermal gradient. Metals have high thermal conductivity k due to free valence electron transport, while insulators rely on slow phonon vibrations.
Place an ice cube on an aluminum pan and another on a plastic cutting board: the pan melts the ice 10x faster due to thermal conductivity!
Thermal Emission Spectra & Wien\'s Displacement Law
Heat an ideal blackbody cavity from 1,000 K to 10,000 K and watch spectral peak shift from infrared to blue.
Heating a metal poker turns it dull red, then cherry red, then bright yellow, and finally blinding white-hot.
Planck resolved the ultraviolet catastrophe by quantizing harmonic oscillator energies (E = nhf). Wien\'s law shows peak emission wavelength is inversely proportional to absolute temperature.
Dim an incandescent light bulb with a dial: notice how the filament color turns from white-yellow to deep orange-red as temperature drops!
Drop a neodymium magnet down a thick copper pipe and watch it fall in eerie slow motion like anti-gravity.
Copper is non-magnetic, yet dropping a magnet down a copper tube makes it fall at a crawl, defying normal free fall.
Moving magnetic fields induce swirling circular eddy currents in conductive copper. By Lenz\'s Law, these currents generate an opposing magnetic field producing a upward braking drag force.
Slide a strong neodymium magnet down a slanted aluminum baking sheet: compare it to sliding a plastic block!
Place a copper wire on top of an AA battery with a neodymium magnet on the bottom and watch the wire spin violently.
A simple dry battery, a magnet, and a bent copper wire create a high-speed spinning motor with zero gears or commutators.
Current flows vertically through the wire and radially outward through the magnetic field lines. The resulting Lorentz force F = I L x B generates continuous rotational torque.
Take an AA battery, stick a neodymium disc magnet to the negative terminal, bend a copper wire into a heart shape over the top!
Charged Particle Motion in Magnetic Fields
Shoot protons and electrons into a perpendicular B-field and watch them curve into circular cyclotron orbits.
Shooting charged particles into empty space filled with a magnetic field causes them to spiral into perfect circles.
Magnetic force is always perpendicular to velocity, doing zero work while providing centripetal acceleration q v B = m v^2 / r, yielding cyclotron radius r = mv / qB.
Look up how cyclotrons in medical hospitals accelerate protons to produce cancer treatment radioactive tracers!
Coil copper wire around an iron core and observe magnetic flux lines pull heavy steel objects inside.
Passing electricity through a coiled wire creates a magnet strong enough to lift scrap cars in a junkyard.
Current circulating through N coil turns concentrates magnetic flux inside the core: B = mu * (N/L) * I. Inserting a ferromagnetic core multiplies field strength by permeability mu_r ~ 5000.
Wrap insulated copper wire 50 times around a large iron nail, connect ends to a 1.5V D-cell battery, and pick up paperclips!
Dual Resonant LC Circuits & Dielectric Breakdown
Tune dual resonant LC tanks to 250 kHz and shoot crackling plasma arcs through the air to illuminate wireless bulbs.
Holding a fluorescent tube near a Tesla coil makes it glow brightly in mid-air with zero wires or batteries.

Two coupled resonant LC circuits tuned to identical frequencies step voltage up to hundreds of thousands of volts, exceeding air dielectric breakdown strength (3 MV/m) and creating branching plasma leaders.
Observe how touch screens and plasma globes use high-frequency electric fields to illuminate neon gas tubes!
Send mega-ampere current pulses down parallel rails to propel an armature projectile to Mach 7 speeds.
Two metal rails and a sliding bar can launch projectiles at hypersonic speeds without using a single grain of gunpowder.
Current traveling down one rail, through the armature, and back down the other rail creates an intense concentrated magnetic field between the rails. The armature experiences immense Lorentz force.
Research naval electromagnetic railgun prototypes that fire kinetic projectiles over 100 miles using pure electrical energy!
Strike a metal mesh sphere with million-volt simulated lightning bolts while the interior remains at absolute zero field.
Sitting inside a metal car struck by a direct lightning bolt leaves you completely unharmed.
Conductors have mobile electrons that rapidly redistribute along the outer surface until internal electric field is precisely zero (E_inside = 0), shielding everything enclosed inside.
Wrap your mobile phone completely in aluminum foil and try calling it from another phone: it loses all signal reception!
Release two double pendulums differing by 0.001Â° and watch their trace paths diverge into wild unpredictability.
A double pendulum governed purely by deterministic Newton\'s laws is completely unpredictable after 5 seconds.
Coupled nonlinear differential equations possess positive Lyapunov exponents lambda > 0, meaning initial infinitesimal uncertainties grow exponentially over time: delta theta(t) ~ e^(lambda t).
Tie two pens end-to-end with string and flick the top pen: notice how the bottom pen spins unpredictably!
Trace the iconic two-lobed butterfly strange attractor discovered by Edward Lorenz in 1963.
A simplified 3-variable weather equation proved that a butterfly flapping its wings in Brazil can set off a tornado in Texas.

A set of 3 coupled non-linear ODEs modelling atmospheric convection produces trajectories that orbit within a bounded region of fractional Hausdorff dimension (~2.06) without ever crossing or repeating.
Explore how weather forecasting is fundamentally limited to 10-14 days due to the chaotic sensitivity of Lorenz dynamics!
Release an iron pendulum above 3 colored attractor magnets and map the intricate fractal destination basins.
Releasing a pendulum above three magnets creates an intricate fractal border where moving the start position by 1 micron changes the final magnet.
The boundary between the three basins of attraction is a fractal boundary with non-integer dimension; near the boundary, any neighborhood contains points leading to all three magnets.
Newtonian Motion in Multi-Well Magnetic Potential
Place three small magnets on a table in a triangle and swing a steel ball on a string directly above them!
Set up initial cell patterns and watch gliders, pulsars, and spaceships emerge from 4 simple rules.
From just 4 simple arithmetic rules of survival and reproduction emerge moving spaceships, self-replicating guns, and universal computers.
John Conway\'s 2D grid cellular automaton demonstrates that simple local deterministic rules can give rise to Turing-complete computational emergence and biological-like complexity.
Draw a 3-cell line on grid paper and update it: watch it oscillate forever as a \'blinker\' period-2 clock!
Start 5 ticking metronomes out of sync on a movable base and watch them spontaneously lock into perfect unison.
